title: HTTP methods

richText: An HTTP method states what the client asks the server to do with a resource.
A resource is something the API identifies with a URL, such as a user or an order.

1: Submit data for processing, often to create a resource.
Create or replace the state at a known resource URL.
Remove the resource at a URL.

richText: The mapping annotation selects the handler. It does not save, replace or delete data itself.
Do not use GET for an operation whose purpose is to change data.
A safe method asks for no change to the resource. GET is safe; server logging can still happen.
An idempotent method has the same intended effect when the same request is repeated.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics. Implement handlers to follow those semantics.
Deleting an already deleted resource does not delete something extra. Its response status can differ from the first response.
POST and PATCH do not guarantee idempotency. A particular API can define repeat-safe behavior for them.
Map the same path to different methods

example.title: Give each user operation its own HTTP mapping
description: These methods belong in a @RestController mapped to /users.
userService is an injected application service. UserResponse and SaveUserRequest are application data classes.
This shows routing only. The service must implement lookup, creation, replacement and deletion.
explanation: GET /users/5 calls find. PUT /users/5 calls replace. DELETE /users/5 calls delete.
@PathVariable reads the identifier from the path. @RequestBody reads the request body.
A POST mapping does not automatically return 201 Created. Choose the status separately with ResponseEntity or @ResponseStatus.
Error responses and explicit success statuses are covered on the ResponseEntity and exception handling pages.

summary: Choose a request method, then understand safe and idempotent operations.
